content: False-negative results can occur with HIV self-testing. Individuals who are HIV-positive but not receiving antiretroviral therapy (ART) should be encouraged and supported to initiate treatment. HIV self-testing allows individuals to test and learn their HIV status privately. Offering a self-testing kit to a sexual partner, friend, or adult family member and encouraging its use can help them determine their HIV status. However, no one should be coerced or forced to self-test, as coercive or mandatory use of self-testing kits is not considered self-testing and should not be supported. The World Health Organization (WHO) advises against parents or guardians using self-testing kits to test infants or children, as these tests are not accurate for children under 18 months due to the presence of maternal antibodies. HIV self-testing kits can be distributed through various channels, including public or donor-funded programs, private sector initiatives, and public-private partnerships. Providing options for service delivery and test kit types (e.g., oral fluid or blood-based kits) can increase accessibility. Distribution models include online ordering with mail delivery, facility-based distribution for later use, community-based campaigns, and integration with existing community testing programs. Retail outlets, pharmacies, vending machines, workplaces, and faith-based settings can also serve as distribution points. Secondary distribution, where individuals distribute kits to their partners or peers, is another effective approach. Support tools, such as video instructions or in-person demonstrations, should be made available to assist individuals in using the kits correctly. HIV partner services, including provider-assisted referral, should be offered as part of a comprehensive testing and care package. Social network-based approaches can also be used to reach key populations and their partners. Despite progress, many people living with HIV remain unaware of their status, particularly in high-risk groups such as men, adolescents, and young people in high-burden areas. Strategic planning is needed to target these populations effectively. Countries should adopt a mix of service delivery approaches tailored to their local context, epidemic nature, and available resources. HIV testing services should prioritize early diagnosis and linkage to care, especially for those at the greatest risk. WHO recommends annual retesting for sexually active individuals in high-burden settings and those with ongoing risk factors, such as key populations or individuals with HIV-positive partners. Pregnant women in high-burden settings should be retested during late pregnancy and postpartum if their status is unknown or negative. Catch-up testing is advised if initial tests are missed or delayed. For infants and children, nucleic acid testing (NAT) at birth can be added to early infant diagnosis strategies in high-burden settings. Routine testing should be offered to children with unknown HIV status who are admitted for inpatient care or attending malnutrition clinics. Point-of-care NAT should be used for children under 18 months, while rapid diagnostic tests can be used for older children following national testing strategies. Key populations, including men who have sex with men, people who inject drugs, sex workers, transgender individuals, and others, should have routine access to HIV testing services in both community and facility-based settings. Adolescents from key populations should also be provided with testing services linked to prevention, treatment, and care. All pregnant women should be tested for HIV, syphilis, and hepatitis B as early as possible during pregnancy. Women experiencing intimate partner violence or sexual assault should receive immediate support, including first-line care from healthcare providers. Post-test services are critical for linking individuals to appropriate care. These services should include clear counseling messages, rapid ART initiation, and connections to prevention and support services. To improve accessibility, HIV testing services should adopt innovative approaches, such as self-testing and partner services, and focus on priority populations and geographical areas. Community-based testing, mobile outreach, and integration with existing health services can effectively reach key populations. Testing for triage using trained lay providers and rapid diagnostic tests can also enhance service delivery.
